questions.stem: In a NSW civil case, who usually carries the burden of proof and to what standard?
options: The judge, on the balance of probabilities
The plaintiff, on the balance of probabilities
The defendant, on the balance of probabilities
The plaintiff, beyond reasonable doubt
questions.explanation: The party bringing the claim, the plaintiff, must prove its case on the balance of probabilities, meaning it is more likely than not. Proof beyond reasonable doubt is the higher criminal standard.

questions.stem: Under the Limitation Act 1969 (NSW), the general time limit for starting a claim for breach of contract is:
options: 6 years from when the cause of action arose
3 years from when the contract was signed
12 months from when the loss was noticed
There is no time limit for any contract claims
questions.explanation: Most contract and tort claims must be started within six years. Personal injury claims generally have a shorter limit of three years from when the claim becomes discoverable, with a 12-year long-stop.

questions.stem: In NSW, the Local Court's Small Claims Division hears civil claims of up to:
questions.explanation: The Small Claims Division deals with claims up to $20,000 in a simple, informal hearing. The Local Court's General Division hears claims over $20,000 and up to $100,000.

questions.stem: Which feature of the Local Court's Small Claims Division makes it more accessible than higher courts?
options: Parties must be represented by a barrister, which ensures the law is applied correctly
Decisions are made by the Chief Justice, so they can never be appealed to another court
Hearings are informal, the strict rules of evidence do not apply and legal costs are limited
Every hearing is decided by a jury, so the parties can rely on community values instead of law
questions.explanation: The Small Claims Division is designed for people to run their own cases cheaply and quickly. Legal representation is not required and there is no jury.

questions.stem: Which NSW court has unlimited jurisdiction in civil matters and can grant equitable remedies in complex disputes?
options: The Children's Court of NSW
The Supreme Court of NSW
The Local Court of NSW
NCAT's Consumer and Commercial Division
questions.explanation: The Supreme Court can hear civil claims of any value and has wide equitable jurisdiction, such as injunctions and specific performance. Lower courts and tribunals have monetary or subject limits.

questions.stem: Jai has a complex commercial dispute worth several million dollars. Why is it likely to be heard in the Supreme Court rather than the Local Court?
options: The Local Court cannot hear any civil claims, because it is limited by statute to criminal and family matters
The Supreme Court is the cheapest court in NSW, so parties always choose it for disputes involving businesses
Only the Supreme Court may use the balance of probabilities, so a lower court could not decide the claim
The claim exceeds the lower courts' monetary limits, and the Supreme Court has the expertise for complex matters
questions.explanation: The court hierarchy allocates cases by value and complexity, allowing specialisation and efficient use of resources. The Local Court hears many civil claims, and the same civil standard of proof applies in every court.

questions.stem: The first document a plaintiff usually files to start civil proceedings in a NSW court is a:
options: charge certificate
statement of claim
court attendance notice
notice of appeal
questions.explanation: A statement of claim sets out the plaintiff's claim and the remedy sought, and the defendant replies with a defence. A court attendance notice and charge certificate are criminal documents.

questions.stem: Before a civil trial, each party must disclose relevant documents to the other. This process is known as:
options: committal
pleading guilty
sentencing
discovery
questions.explanation: Discovery lets each side see the documents relevant to the case, reducing surprise and encouraging settlement. Committal and sentencing are criminal processes.

questions.stem: Under section 56 of the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW), the overriding purpose of civil procedure is to:
options: allow parties as much time as they wish to prepare without any court deadlines
facilitate the just, quick and cheap resolution of the real issues in the proceedings
ensure that every civil dispute is decided at a full trial before a jury of twelve
guarantee that each party has the same number of lawyers and the same budget
questions.explanation: The overriding purpose supports active case management, such as timetables and referrals to mediation, to reduce delay and cost. It does not require jury trials or equal resources.

questions.stem: A party makes a formal written offer to settle a civil case before trial, and the other party refuses it but then does worse at trial. What is the likely consequence?
options: The party who made the offer must pay all the costs because the offer was not accepted
The trial must be restarted with a new judge because the offer was refused
The party who refused may be ordered to pay more of the other side's legal costs
The party who refused will automatically have the court's judgment set aside
questions.explanation: Offers of compromise encourage early settlement, because a party who unreasonably rejects an offer and then does worse can face adverse costs orders. The usual rule is that costs follow the event, so the loser pays much of the winner's costs.

questions.stem: Under the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW), a group of seven or more people with claims arising from the same circumstances against the same defendant can bring a:
options: merits review application at NCAT against the defendant
representative proceeding (class action) in the Supreme Court
private prosecution in the Local Court before a magistrate
royal commission into the defendant's conduct and business practices
questions.explanation: Representative proceedings, available in the NSW Supreme Court since 2011, let one representative sue for a whole group, which improves access to justice for people with small individual claims. Royal commissions and merits review are not ways for private parties to sue a defendant.

questions.stem: The NSW Civil and Administrative Tribunal (NCAT) began operating in:
questions.explanation: NCAT began on 1 January 2014, bringing more than 20 tribunals into one body with divisions such as Consumer and Commercial, Administrative and Equal Opportunity, and Guardianship. It provides a cheaper and quicker alternative to the courts.

questions.stem: Mei's landlord refuses to return her bond, claiming damage she says she did not cause. Where should she take the dispute?
options: The NSW Court of Criminal Appeal
The Federal Court of Australia
NCAT's Consumer and Commercial Division
The Supreme Court of NSW in its equity division
questions.explanation: NCAT hears residential tenancy, consumer, home building and strata disputes, generally without lawyers and at low cost. The Court of Criminal Appeal deals only with criminal matters.

questions.stem: Which statement best compares NCAT with the courts as a way of resolving civil disputes?
options: NCAT is cheaper, faster and less formal, but it has limited jurisdiction and its orders may need a court to enforce
NCAT is more formal than the Supreme Court and always requires both parties to be represented by barristers
NCAT can hear any civil claim of any value, which makes the Local, District and Supreme Courts unnecessary
NCAT decisions are made by juries, which makes them more consistent than decisions of judges in the courts
questions.explanation: Tribunals improve access to justice through low fees and simple procedures, but they deal only with the matters their legislation gives them. Some NCAT money orders are enforced through the Local Court.

questions.stem: Community Justice Centres in NSW provide:
options: free legal representation in criminal trials heard before a jury in the District Court of NSW
investigations of complaints made against government departments and their officers
free, voluntary and confidential mediation for disputes such as those between neighbours
binding judgments in civil disputes worth more than one million dollars across NSW
questions.explanation: Community Justice Centres, set up under the Community Justice Centres Act 1983 (NSW), offer mediation by trained mediators to help parties reach their own agreement. Complaints about government agencies go to the Ombudsman.

questions.stem: Under the Civil Procedure Act 2005 (NSW), a NSW court may refer a case to mediation:
options: only if the dispute is worth less than $1,000
with or without the consent of the parties
only if both parties have signed a contract
only after the trial has been fully completed
questions.explanation: Courts can order parties to attempt mediation, which is part of active case management aimed at early settlement. The parties still decide whether to settle; mediators do not impose outcomes.

questions.stem: Two companies agree that an expert will hear their building dispute in private and make a binding decision. Which method of dispute resolution is this?
options: Negotiation
Arbitration
Mediation
Conciliation
questions.explanation: In arbitration an independent arbitrator hears evidence and makes a binding decision, often more privately and flexibly than a court. In mediation and conciliation the parties reach their own agreement.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates alternative dispute resolution as a way of achieving justice in civil disputes?
options: It always produces a binding judgment that sets a precedent, so it develops the law faster than the courts can
It is more formal than a trial and requires lawyers, so it is less accessible than going to court for most people
It can only be used after a court has decided who is liable, so it adds to the time and cost of every dispute
It is cheaper and can preserve relationships, but it may be unfair where one party has much more power or information
questions.explanation: ADR is accessible and lets parties control the outcome, but a power imbalance can lead to an unfair agreement, and private settlements do not set precedents. Courts may still be needed where one party will not cooperate.

questions.stem: Which method of dispute resolution involves the parties discussing the dispute directly with each other, without an independent third party?
options: Negotiation
Arbitration
Mediation
Litigation
questions.explanation: Negotiation is the most informal and cheapest method, used before or alongside other methods. Mediation and arbitration involve a third party, and litigation involves a court.

questions.stem: In a NSW civil case, the party who starts the proceedings is called the:
options: plaintiff
prosecutor
accused
respondent to a charge
questions.explanation: The plaintiff sues the defendant to seek a remedy. Prosecutors and accused persons are parties in criminal cases.

questions.stem: What is the main role of a judge in a civil trial heard without a jury in NSW?
options: To present evidence on behalf of the party with the stronger case
To decide only the law, leaving the facts to the parties' lawyers
To negotiate a settlement on behalf of the parties outside court
To decide the facts and the law, determine liability and order a remedy
questions.explanation: In a judge-alone civil trial, which is the usual form in NSW, the judge decides both facts and law and gives reasons. As an impartial umpire, the judge does not argue for either side.

questions.stem: What is the difference between the roles of a solicitor and a barrister in a civil case?
options: A solicitor works for the court; a barrister works for the government department that is involved in the case
A solicitor usually advises the client and prepares the case; a barrister usually presents it in court
A solicitor decides the outcome of the case; a barrister enforces the judgment once it has been made
A solicitor represents the plaintiff only; a barrister represents only the defendant in civil cases
questions.explanation: Solicitors handle the client relationship, paperwork and preparation, and often brief a barrister for advocacy in higher courts. Either side may use both kinds of lawyer.

questions.stem: Which statement about civil juries in NSW is correct?
options: Civil juries decide the law and the judge decides only the facts and the amount of damages
Civil juries are made up of lawyers chosen by the parties from a list kept by the court
Most civil trials are heard by a judge alone, but a jury of four can be used in some cases
Every civil trial must be heard by a jury of twelve, as in criminal trials for serious offences
questions.explanation: Civil proceedings in NSW are usually heard without a jury unless the court orders one, and a civil jury normally has four members. In defamation cases a party can generally elect to have a jury.

questions.stem: A NSW civil jury of four has deliberated for more than four hours without reaching a unanimous verdict. Under the Jury Act 1977 (NSW), what may happen?
options: The plaintiff automatically wins because the jury could not agree
The case is sent to the High Court for a final decision
A verdict agreed by three of the four jurors may be accepted
The judge must decide the case alone and dismiss the jury
questions.explanation: Section 57 of the Jury Act allows a majority verdict of three of four jurors in a civil case after more than four hours of deliberation. If no such verdict is reached, the jury may be discharged.

questions.stem: In a NSW defamation trial with a jury, what is the main role of the jury?
options: To decide whether the defendant has been proved to have defamed the plaintiff and whether a defence applies
To decide the amount of damages the defendant must pay, while the judge decides whether a defamation occurred
To investigate the case by questioning witnesses who have not been called by either of the parties
To decide which laws apply to the case after hearing arguments from the barristers for each party
questions.explanation: Under the Defamation Act 2005 (NSW), the jury decides whether the defendant published defamatory matter and whether any defence is established, while the judge decides damages. Juries decide facts, not law.

questions.stem: What is the main aim of civil remedies?
options: To raise revenue for the government through penalties paid by losing parties
To deter all other members of society from going to court over minor disputes
To restore the plaintiff, as far as possible, to the position they were in before the wrong
To punish the defendant with imprisonment for the harm done to the community
questions.explanation: Civil remedies mainly compensate the plaintiff or stop a continuing wrong. Punishment is the aim of criminal sanctions, although exemplary damages occasionally punish very bad conduct.

questions.stem: After a car accident, a court awards Lily an amount for her past medical bills and lost wages, which can be calculated exactly. These are:
options: special damages
general damages
nominal damages
exemplary damages
questions.explanation: Special damages cover losses that can be precisely calculated, such as bills and lost earnings to the date of trial. General damages compensate for things that cannot be calculated exactly, such as pain and suffering.

questions.stem: Under the Civil Liability Act 2002 (NSW), what limit applies to damages for non-economic loss, such as pain and suffering, in a personal injury negligence claim?
options: They are unlimited, because a jury may award any amount it considers fair in every negligence case
They may be awarded only where the defendant has also been convicted of a crime in a criminal court
They are always set at exactly half of the plaintiff's special damages for medical and other expenses
They are available only if the loss is at least 15 per cent of a most extreme case, and are capped
questions.explanation: The Act sets a threshold of 15 per cent of a most extreme case and a maximum amount, introduced in 2002 to reduce insurance costs. Critics argue this can leave some injured people under-compensated.

questions.stem: A court orders a seller to complete the sale of a rare painting as agreed in a contract, because money would not be an adequate remedy. This remedy is:
options: rescission
specific performance
an interim injunction
nominal damages
questions.explanation: Specific performance is an equitable remedy ordering a party to carry out a contract, used where damages would be inadequate, such as for unique items or land. Rescission cancels a contract instead of enforcing it.

questions.stem: A buyer was persuaded to sign a contract by the seller's misrepresentation. The court sets the contract aside and returns both parties to their original positions. This remedy is:
options: specific performance
general damages
a mandatory injunction
rescission
questions.explanation: Rescission cancels a contract affected by matters such as misrepresentation or undue influence, undoing it as far as possible. Specific performance would enforce the contract instead.

questions.stem: A low-income person with a strong claim against a large company abandons it because she cannot risk paying the company's legal costs if she loses. Which concept of justice is most clearly undermined?
options: Access to justice, because cost discourages people from using the legal system
The presumption of innocence, because the company is assumed to be in the wrong
The right to silence, because she is forced to give evidence against herself
Procedural fairness, because the judge refuses to hear the company's evidence
questions.explanation: The costs rule means losing parties usually pay the winner's costs, which deters people with limited means from suing, even with strong cases. The presumption of innocence and the right to silence belong to criminal law.

questions.stem: Which statement best evaluates how well the NSW civil justice system achieves equality?
options: Every party receives a free lawyer from the state in civil cases, so wealth has no effect on the outcome of litigation
Civil courts must always rule in favour of the party with fewer resources, which guarantees equal outcomes for everyone
Equality is not relevant in civil law, because only criminal courts must treat the parties in the same way
Tribunals, ADR and small claims procedures help, but wealthier parties can still afford better lawyers and longer litigation
questions.explanation: Equality before the law means the same rules apply to all, but in practice resources affect the ability to run a case. Legal aid for civil matters is very limited, so lower-cost forums are important.
